svg.text: The piece funnels one worry (work disappearing) into three parallel historical case studies that converge on the
same pattern — dignity from group status, not achievement — then follows a chain explaining why ordinary paid work
escapes that trap, looping back at the end to the fear it opened with.

g.text: After Work, We'll Have Each Other
Three historical case studies converge on one pattern, which a closing chain uses to explain — and worry about losing —
what paid work actually gives us.

g.title: When AI ends work, relationships supply status — the relational-sector thesis — If machines do all economically necessary labor, the argument goes, humans fall back on relationships for status and meaning. — → spya-eq7rkm
Versailles ran on petty status feuds, not ideas — Saint-Simon's memoirs show courtiers obsessed with heraldic precedence over culture or philosophy. — → spya-y827zc
Etiquette curbed — not proved — ape instincts — Elias: court ceremony was a civilizing restraint on primate dominance behavior, not its inevitable expression. — → spya-cz0cgg
Lives built around defending class standing — Ostrander's 1980s subjects never worked and organized life around keeping their social network 'in good order.' — → spya-uum3xk
Charity valued for its 'illusion of usefulness' — Board fundraising mattered for status, not for measurable results — by the women's own admission. — → spya-mdncme
Peer groups and gossip ruled over dead-end jobs — Gans's Boston Italian-Americans spent as little time at work as possible, organizing life around close peer groups. — → spya-y02mr5
Amoral familism faded as options improved — Distrust of outsiders was a rational response to poverty, and it receded as material conditions changed. — → spya-dma27v

Status comes from the group, not achievement — Across courts, old money, and peer groups, dignity depends on group membership, which makes every society of this kind clannish and exclusive. — → spya-qsfkqr
Work gives impersonal respect, not just money — Unlike group-based honor, work lets you earn dignity for what you do, not who you know. — → spya-zd83ts

Surveys and oral histories: workers want respect — From Pew surveys to Studs Terkel's interviews, workers consistently value feeling competent and respected over enjoying the task itself. — → spya-t9qyhk
Commercial society freed friendship from necessity — Because relational societies struggle with equality, the market's loosening of feudal and family ties let friendship become freer. — → spya-hdbtc0
Author's wary hope: liberal individualism survives — The author likes her job and liberal individualism, and hopes that if a relational world is coming, it won't cost us the latter. — → spya-dhj4jr
Notes & further reading (sources, citations) — → spya-u4ztzw

g.text: A chain of escalating evidence that aristocratic life without work was petty and status-obsessed, ending with a caveat
that this need not be our fate.

g.title: Versailles: Europe's wealthiest, most brilliant court — Voltaire called it one of history's four great ages of light — yet its culture was dominated by status games. — → spya-gs52t3
Saint-Simon obsessed over heraldic precedence — His memoirs devote hundreds of pages to disputes over emblems and ceremonial headgear, not culture or ideas. — → spya-x4w0zk
Salons were gossip, not philosophy — Despite their Enlightenment reputation, salon attendees mostly talked politics and each other, not ideas. — → spya-wue7zn
Lilti: salon talk was mostly political gossip — → spya-k0yet6
Catherine's Petersburg: same gossip-driven pattern — Even a brilliant, pragmatic ruler's court ran on tracking who offended whom to gain favor. — → spya-f90g2h
Aristocratic dignity: honor, not diligence — Bourgeois dignity comes from being productive; aristocratic dignity comes from maintaining rank and family distinction. — → spya-de69sf
Aristocrats act like status-obsessed chimpanzees — Constant tracking of alliances, challenges, and displays of rank resembles primate dominance hierarchies. — → spya-cz0cgg
Elias: civilizing, not fixed, instinct — we might do better — Versailles behavior reflected centuries of specific feudal institutions, not an inevitable return to primate nature. — → spya-k26ath

g.text: Four kinds of evidence feed one claim about what work supplies, which then explains why commercial society freed
friendship — and the author's wary conclusion.

g.title: Work supplies impersonal respect and competence — The central claim: paid work's main gift, besides money, is a way to earn dignity for what you do rather than who you know. — → spya-zd83ts
85% of workers report job satisfaction — Pew, Gallup, and The Conference Board surveys agree, even for unglamorous jobs. — → spya-sw09bu
Strauss: COVID return showed pride, relief — Workers returning from lockdown spoke of feeling useful again, not of loving their tasks. — → spya-nm9v43
FWP interviews: work mattered as much as family — Depression-era life stories rated pride in work and recognition by peers alongside family and community. — → spya-a5pt8y
Terkel's Working: respect beat job content — 1970s Chicago workers hated disrespect far more than repetition, and prized being useful to peers. — → spya-n00hd0
Relational societies struggle with moral equality — When dignity depends on group membership, societies get clannish — policing who belongs and who doesn't. — → spya-hdbtc0
Commercial society freed friendship from necessity — Smith, Hume, and Ferguson argued that once labor meets our needs, friendship can rest on sympathy rather than transaction. — → spya-tmepex
Author's wary hope: liberal individualism survives — If a more relational future is coming, the author hopes we keep the freedom commercial society gave our relationships. — → spya-dhj4jr
